Frederick stared at the glowing runes, the weight of eternity pressing against his mortal heart. The draft from the hidden chamber grew colder, carrying with it the scent of decay and ancient dust. He looked at the list of ingredients—rare, dangerous, and morally ambiguous. To drink the potion was to step outside the natural order, to become a ghost in the living world, watching everyone he loved turn to dust while he remained unchanged.

He thought of his daughter, whose laughter had been the only light in his dark years of scholarship. If he chose immortality, he would lose her memory, her touch, and her very existence, all while he remained a static observer. The temptation was a physical ache, but the horror of the alternative was greater.

With a trembling hand, Frederick did not reach for the vial. Instead, he reached for the edge of the parchment. He held it over the brazier burning in the center of the altar. The runes seemed to pulse, warning him, begging him to stop. But Frederick whispered a final prayer, not for life, but for peace. He dropped the parchment into the flames.

The fire did not just burn the paper; it consumed the magic. The runes flared bright white, then faded into ash. The sudden draft ceased, and the chamber fell into a profound, silent stillness. Frederick felt a sudden lightness, as if a burden he hadn’t known he was carrying had been lifted. He was mortal, he was finite, and he was free. He turned and walked out of the hidden chamber, leaving the secret of eternal life to the dark, where it belonged.

***

**Priority Question Answer:** Christopher Columbus
